title: Scholarship & learning
summary: To learn a new language is to make a larger world available.
source: The scholar example, Idea 1; vocabulary example, Idea 2.

sections.heading: Knowledge as extension
sections.body:
The scholar extends the self through knowledge. A language might be English or Arabic, but it might also be mathematics or code: a way to encounter people, ideas, or natural laws beyond immediate experience.

Consider the difference between seeing an unfamiliar formula and being able to read it. Before learning its language, the marks offer little access to the relationship they describe. Afterward, the same page becomes a way to think with people one has never met and about things one cannot directly see. The scholar’s world grows because there is now another kind of conversation they can enter.

A new vocabulary can make an experience intelligible and shareable. But jargon can also close a door when it becomes a requirement for being heard. The same tool that extends one person can exclude another.

Learning matters when it changes what someone can notice, question, or do. Memorizing a technical term adds little if it cannot be connected to an experience. Teaching that term through an example turns private expertise into shared access: the learner gains a way to participate and the teacher gains a person with whom to think.

That possibility also gives expertise a responsibility. If understanding is a form of reach, explaining an idea clearly allows that reach to be shared. A useful question for the scholar is what their knowledge makes available to someone else: a better question, a way to challenge an assumption, or enough confidence to begin learning for themselves.

question: Who can now participate in a conversation that was previously closed to them?

title: Wealth & influence
summary: When self-worth depends on accumulation, what would ever count as enough?
source: The CEO example, Idea 1; power as language, Idea 3.

sections.heading: An expanding sphere of influence
sections.body:
The CEO example describes self-extension through wealth and power: the ability to affect a world larger than the individual body. In this reading, money matters partly for the reach it makes possible.

The distinction between security and status matters here. Being able to pay for a necessity changes the conditions of daily life. Being able to rank above another person changes a comparison. Both may feel like progress, but only the first has an obvious stopping point. When the comparison becomes the goal, a larger sphere of influence can leave the original anxiety intact.

Under the hedonic premise, accumulation needs to be evaluated by the pain it relieves and produces. Horace’s Satire 1.1 offers a related question about discontent: does pursuing more actually make life more livable? (Horace, n.d.).

Money can remove concrete burdens: uncertainty about housing, food, time, or care. Beyond that relief, accumulation can become a way to measure worth against other people. The threshold then moves whenever someone else has more. Evaluate influence by what it enables and whom it affects, as well as by how far it reaches.

Influence also changes how much explanation a person must offer. Someone who controls an opportunity may be able to issue a short instruction while others spend time anticipating what will satisfy them. The draft’s connection between power and language invites us to count this unequal work alongside the visible signs of success.

question: Is this ambition enlarging a life, or making contentment permanently unreachable?

title: Travel
summary: A physical journey can become an expansion of the self.

sections.heading: Beyond the immediate surroundings
sections.body:
Travel is physical self-extension. A person moves beyond the familiar room and meets places, people, and ways of living that were previously outside their experience.

Imagine arriving somewhere with enough vocabulary to buy a ticket but little ability to ask about the lives around you. The physical journey has happened; much of the social world remains inaccessible. Learning how to ask, listen, and accept correction can turn a location into an encounter with someone whose experience differs from your own.

Movement alone does not ensure understanding. The model directs attention to how a traveler communicates, whose language is expected, and whether an encounter allows mutual recognition.

The lasting extension happens when an encounter changes how the familiar is understood. A traveler may return with different assumptions about hospitality, time, or ordinary life. Collecting destinations offers one measure of movement; being able to describe another person’s circumstances with greater care offers a measure of understanding.

The traveler can also notice who makes that encounter possible. If every conversation takes place in the traveler’s language, another person is doing the work of translation. Recognizing that work changes the meaning of exploration: reaching outward involves being willing to adjust one’s own habits and expectations.

question: Does this encounter expand understanding on both sides?

title: Religion & spirituality
summary: Self-extension can reach toward something understood as larger than the self.
source: The priest example, Idea 1; explicitly tentative in the founding essay.

sections.heading: A spiritual horizon
sections.body:
Religious practice can extend a person’s world through prayer, ritual, community, and a relationship to what they understand as sacred. Self-extension here involves belonging and meaning as well as reach.

The priest in the original essay is a tentative example of reaching beyond the immediately visible world. Prayer or ritual may connect a person to a higher power, a community, or a sense of continuity beyond an individual lifetime. Understanding that example requires listening to how the participant describes the connection, rather than assuming every tradition seeks the same kind of expansion.

Spiritual traditions differ in what they understand a self to be. The model begins with how a person describes their practice and asks what it makes possible: connection, obligation, consolation, or a new way of understanding the world.

A shared ritual connects an individual life to other people and to a history. That connection can carry comfort and responsibility at once. To understand it, ask what the practice asks of the participant, what support it provides, and whether participation leaves room for questions and choice.

This also complicates the language of “more.” A practice might ask someone to relinquish status or loosen their attachment to an individual identity. The model becomes useful when it can accommodate that account of meaning, rather than treating wealth, knowledge, and spiritual life as interchangeable things to accumulate.

question: How does this person describe their own spiritual form of self-extension?

title: Love & relationships
summary: To love someone is, in part, to experience a world through their eyes.
source: The lover example, Idea 1; relationships in the closing examples.

sections.heading: A self that includes another
sections.body:
A loved person becomes part of one’s world: we experience life through our own eyes and, in another sense, through theirs. This applies to friendship as well as romance.

Sharing another person’s world happens through ordinary acts of attention. Learning why a place matters to them, listening to a memory, or understanding an unfamiliar fear gives an experience significance it did not have before. Their perspective becomes something you can carry into your own decisions, while remaining a perspective they can revise or explain differently.

The model assumes a relationship on equal footing needs reciprocal communication. Expecting someone to guess an unspoken feeling shifts the entire burden of understanding onto them. Naming a feeling gives the other person a chance to respond.

Including another person in one’s world does not make their agency an extension of one’s own will. A relationship grows when both people can express a need, refuse a demand, and maintain connections beyond the relationship. Care expands the worlds available to each person; control makes one world depend on the other’s permission.

This is why the draft connects equal footing with the willingness to communicate. If one person’s feelings must always be guessed while the other’s must always be justified, the work of closeness has become unequal. Mutual understanding takes participation from both people, including the ability to say that an interpretation is wrong or a request cannot be met.

question: Where am I asking to be understood without helping someone understand?

title: Illness & the shrinking world
summary: Pain can pull a vast world back into the confines of a room.

sections.heading: When the world contracts
sections.body:
The fever example makes contraction concrete. While severely ill, someone may find that work, travel, wealth, and abstract ideas recede as bodily pain takes over attention. This image develops Scarry’s (1985) account of pain and the contraction of a world.

The room in the draft is a concrete image of a shrinking world. Plans and relationships may still exist, yet feel impossibly distant when the body demands attention. What has changed is the person’s access to those possibilities. A world that was available yesterday can become difficult to enter today.

Within the model, reducing pain can restore the possibility of attending to something beyond the body. This is a conceptual account of experience, not a claim that every form of pain has one cause or response.

A task that once seemed small can become difficult when pain occupies attention. The loss is not only the task itself, but the ability to imagine and pursue what comes next. Practical support can reduce that burden by making the immediate surroundings more manageable, without requiring the person to turn suffering into a lesson.

That image helps explain why relief has significance beyond the moment of comfort. Making food available, reducing a practical demand, or offering company on someone’s terms can leave more room for attention elsewhere. The relevant question is what the person wants to regain access to, rather than what an observer thinks they should accomplish.

question: What would give this person room to attend to the world again?

title: Pedagogy
summary: Education gives us words for the world—and for what happens inside us.

sections.heading: Three tasks of education
sections.body:
Schools should cultivate academic learning, emotional intelligence, and moral reasoning. Knowing how to acquire information is only one part of knowing how to live with other people.

The original essay gives education three connected tasks: academic learning, emotional intelligence, and moral reasoning. Each enlarges what a student can recognize. A method helps them investigate a problem; emotional vocabulary helps them describe an experience; a worked example of conduct helps them reason about what happened between people.

Examples give students language for recognizing harm and healthy relationships. This connects to Horace’s Satire 1.4, where a father teaches through concrete examples and the speaker later examines his own conduct. The connection is interpretive, not a claim that Horace proposed this whole model. (Horace, n.d.).

A student who can name coercion or distinguish criticism from humiliation has a more precise way to interpret an encounter. The lesson becomes useful when they can apply it to an unfamiliar case and explain their reasoning. Education extends agency by making both recognition and response possible.

For a student whose familiar surroundings make harmful behavior seem ordinary, another example can matter enormously. A classroom can offer language for a relationship in which disagreement is possible and boundaries are respected. The words become useful through discussion and comparison, as students learn to explain why an example fits and where the distinction becomes difficult.

question: What experience could a student recognize and communicate after this lesson?

title: Politics & rhetoric
summary: The words used to name harm can also be used to conceal it.
source: Politics, Idea 2; global language and courts, Idea 3.

sections.heading: The power to frame an event
sections.body:
Consider what happens when an institution redescribes harm so that it no longer appears to count as harm. In the model, denying someone the vocabulary for their experience can obstruct recognition and repair.

A description directs attention. Calling an action necessary, accidental, or deserved invites different questions about responsibility and repair. The draft asks us to examine what happens when a description makes inflicted pain disappear from the account. If the harm cannot be acknowledged in the language an institution accepts, the route to addressing it becomes harder to enter.

Idea 3 examines power through what someone does not have to do. Whose language is treated as the default? Who must translate, explain, or prove their pain? These are questions for examining institutions, rather than evidence about any particular event.

Naming a harm matters because it can make a shared response possible. Recognition alone does not redistribute resources, change a procedure, or repair an injury. Trace the path from a description to a decision: who is heard, who can challenge the account, and who has the authority to act on it?

The same problem appears in the language of a hearing or complaint. Someone may have an experience to describe but lack the vocabulary treated as authoritative. An institution can help make that account understandable, or make recognition depend on the speaker doing all the translation. That choice reveals whose understanding the process is built around.

question: Whose account of what happened is allowed to define the situation?

title: Violence
summary: Violence uses force or power to impose harm. Understanding it begins with who bears the consequences.
source: Background thought; the founding essay’s original model of violence.

sections.heading: Force, power, and harm
sections.body:
Violence involves intentional force or power, threatened or actual, that causes or is likely to cause injury, death, psychological harm, or deprivation (Krug et al., 2002). Pain is an experience; violence is an action or exercise of power. Illness can hurt without violence, while coercion can cause harm without leaving a visible wound.

The draft begins with an attempt to understand how an internal feeling becomes an outward action. When a person cannot make distress intelligible, force may appear to offer an immediate way to make it felt. This is a question about one possible route from pain to action; deliberate coercion and other motives require attention as well.

Some violence can be understood as a physical expression of overwhelming internal feeling that has not found a communicable form. Examine preexisting pain, the pain an action causes, and the pain that remains.

This is an interpretive possibility, not a universal cause of violence. Explaining an action does not justify it. Shared vocabulary may help communicate distress, but language alone cannot guarantee safety or remove responsibility for harm.

An act of intimidation may reduce the aggressor’s uncertainty by forcing compliance. The apparent relief is purchased by transferring fear and constraint to another person. A calculus limited to the aggressor misses the central harm. Follow the consequences across people and across time, including the choices the harmed person can no longer make freely.

Following the action through time prevents that explanation from stopping with the person who acted. What changed for the person threatened or hurt? What fear now shapes their choices? A moment that feels resolving to one participant can begin a much longer burden for another. The model has to include both experiences to explain the encounter adequately.

question: What pain preceded this action, and who is now carrying its consequences?

title: Incel culture & dominance
summary: What happens when expressing emotion is devalued and dominance is rewarded?
source: Incels example in the closing applications.

sections.heading: A narrowed vocabulary
sections.body:
Social media can circulate messages that dismiss emotional expression and elevate dominance. Read through this model, such messages can narrow the available ways to communicate vulnerability or seek recognition.

The draft is concerned with messages that make emotional expression seem worthless while presenting dominance as a route to recognition. In that vocabulary, admitting loneliness can be treated as defeat. A person then has fewer accepted ways to ask for connection, while hostility may become a way to demonstrate membership in the group.

The entry concerns the pattern of silencing vulnerability, not every person associated with a label. The useful question is how a community’s language can encourage care or normalize causing pain.

Loneliness and humiliation deserve to be heard. They do not create a claim on another person’s attention, affection, or body. A community can help its members describe rejection and build connection, or teach them to interpret another person’s autonomy as an injury. Those responses lead to very different relationships with the world.

Examining that language means asking what kinds of response the community rewards. Does someone who expresses grief receive room to reflect, or pressure to turn it into blame? The distinction matters because support can acknowledge pain while leaving other people free to choose their own relationships.

question: What ways of expressing vulnerability does this community make possible?

title: Misunderstanding
summary: An unspoken feeling becomes a story someone else has to invent.
source: The drama and misunderstanding subpoint under relationships.

sections.heading: The missing explanation
sections.body:
Misunderstandings in dramas offer a familiar illustration: people act on interpretations they have not checked. Their internal experience is real, but it has not become shared knowledge.

A familiar dramatic scene makes the mechanism clear: someone leaves without explaining why, and the person left behind supplies a motive. The explanation may feel certain because it fits an existing fear. Yet the event and the meaning assigned to it are separate pieces of information, and only one has been shared.

The model suggests asking what each person knows, what they assume, and what remains unsaid. Clarification may reduce avoidable pain, while differences in values or interests can persist even after perfect understanding.

One person may interpret silence as rejection while another understands it as a pause to recover. Saying what the silence means changes the information available to both. If the conflict persists after that clarification, its source may be a difference in needs or boundaries that requires a decision, rather than another explanation.

A clarification makes that gap visible. Asking what happened, saying what one understood, and allowing the answer to change the interpretation can interrupt the story before it becomes another action. This requires enough trust to ask and enough willingness to answer; neither person gains access to the other’s inner life simply by feeling strongly about it.

question: Which part of the conflict rests on an assumption nobody has checked?

title: Bullying & silencing
summary: Being hurt and being unable to speak about it can compound one another.
source: Bullying and the quiet child in the closing examples.

sections.heading: Pain without an audience
sections.body:
A person can be hurt and then told to remain quiet. Within the model, silencing removes a possible route to recognition and leaves the person with fewer ways to communicate distress.

Silencing can happen after the original incident: a complaint is dismissed as oversensitivity, a witness avoids involvement, or the person targeted is told that speaking will make things worse. The experience then includes both the hurt and the difficulty of getting anyone to recognize it. The available world shrinks when ordinary participation comes to carry the expectation of humiliation.

Unaddressed pain can lead to further harm. That is a hypothesis about a possible cycle, not a prediction that bullied people become violent. A response should recognize the original harm and preserve everyone’s responsibility for their actions.

An invitation to speak is incomplete if speaking brings retaliation or changes nothing. Recognition requires a listener who can respond, protect room for the account, and address the behavior causing harm. The burden should not fall on the targeted person to become more articulate before anyone takes the situation seriously.

The draft’s concern with uncommunicated pain directs attention to the conditions of being heard. Having words is useful when there is someone willing and able to listen. A response must also address the repeated conduct and the consequences of reporting it, so that expression becomes a route toward change rather than another occasion for exposure.

question: Who can hear this person without dismissing or punishing their account?

title: Parenting
summary: Between absence and control lies the work of helping another person grow.
source: Parenting example in the closing applications.

sections.heading: Two limiting cases
sections.body:
Compare parents who offer little communication with parents who communicate through excessive control. One withholds support; the other risks crowding out a child’s ability to develop a world of their own.

The two extremes in the draft reveal different obstacles to growth. With little communication, a child may be left to interpret difficult experiences without help. With constant control, the child may have explanations imposed on every experience and little opportunity to develop a judgment of their own. Both raise the question of what kind of world the child is being allowed to enter.

Through the model, parenting can be evaluated by whether words help a child recognize feelings, understand consequences, and develop agency. Care requires attention to the child’s needs, growing independence, and circumstances.

Explaining a boundary gives a child something they can eventually use without the parent present. As their understanding grows, choices and responsibilities can grow with it. The question is whether a rule builds the ability to judge a situation or merely teaches the child to wait for permission.

An ordinary disagreement can become practice in that growing capacity. A parent can explain a limit, hear how the child understands it, and help connect an action to its consequences. Over time, that exchange gives the child language they can use in situations where the parent is absent, including language for questioning a demand.

question: Are these words helping a child develop their own capacity to understand and act?

title: Abuse & obstructed agency
summary: Power can be used to restrict another person’s world.
source: Abuse example; unequal commands in Idea 3.

sections.heading: Blocking another person’s extension
sections.body:
Someone frustrated in their own self-extension may seek to prevent another person’s growth. Isolation, control, and punishment can be examined here as restrictions on another person’s agency.

The draft proposes a pattern in which someone responds to frustration by limiting another person’s extension. The other person’s friendships, ambitions, or independent judgments become things to suppress. This lens directs attention to the narrowing of possibilities and to the way control can be presented as concern or loyalty.

This is one proposed interpretation, not a complete account of abuse. The responsibility belongs to the person causing harm. Better communication by the harmed person is not an obligation or a guarantee that coercion will stop.

A restriction on friendships, money, movement, or speech can make ordinary decisions depend on another person’s approval. The loss of agency is part of the harm, even when the restriction is described as care. Evaluate the pattern by whose options shrink and who gains the ability to decide for them.

Language can participate in that narrowing when every objection must be defended and every restriction is treated as self-evident. One person is required to explain more and more while the person imposing the restriction offers less. Looking at that unequal burden helps make the structure of control visible alongside its individual incidents.

question: Whose ability to connect, choose, or speak is being restricted?

title: Art & expression
summary: A feeling can become a movement, an image, or a page.
source: Art example in the closing applications.

sections.heading: Language beyond speech
sections.body:
Dance, visual art, and writing are forms of language. They can give an internal experience an external form, making something available to a viewer, a reader, or even the maker themselves.

An experience need not begin as a sentence. A rhythm, gesture, image, or arrangement of space can carry something the maker has struggled to articulate. In the draft’s broad definition of language, these forms matter because they allow an inner experience to take shape outside the body, where it can be encountered again.

Through this model, making art is a form of self-extension and a possible means of relief. That possibility does not imply that all art heals or that an experience must be made public to matter.

Making an experience tangible can help a person revisit it at a different distance. A private page and a public performance offer different possibilities for recognition. The maker retains the choice of audience: expression can enlarge a world without making every part of an inner life available to everyone.

The audience also brings a vocabulary to that encounter. A movement may be immediately meaningful to one viewer and unfamiliar to another. Expression does not guarantee identical understanding, but it can open a conversation that ordinary explanation has not opened. Even an incomplete recognition can offer a new point of contact.

question: What can this form express that ordinary speech has not been able to carry?

title: Learning & association
summary: Experience shapes what we expect, what we approach, and what we avoid.
source: An extension of the original model. Sources: OpenStax, Psychology 2e, sections 6.2–6.3; Purves et al., Neuroscience, Mechanism of Long-Term Synaptic Plasticity; O’Doherty, Reward Predictions and Computations. References are linked in the home page’s Sources & notes.

sections.heading: Learning what to expect
sections.body:
Classical conditioning concerns learning relationships between events. A cue that predicts an outcome can come to elicit a response of its own. Within this model, that helps explain how a word, place, or tone of voice could come to signal anticipated pain or comfort (Spielman et al., 2020).

It helps to distinguish a cue from a consequence in the same example. A particular tone of voice might predict an argument and bring anxiety before a conversation begins. Leaving the room might then reduce that anxiety. The first relationship concerns what predicts what; the second concerns what follows an action and whether that result makes the action more likely.

Operant conditioning concerns actions and their consequences. Reinforcement increases a behavior; punishment decreases it. Avoiding a conversation may remove anxiety. If that relief makes future avoidance more likely, this is negative reinforcement. Relief now can coexist with an unresolved problem later (Spielman et al., 2020).

Synaptic plasticity includes changes in the strength of connections between neurons and contributes to learning and memory. Some dopamine signals track differences between expected and received rewards. These mechanisms help us examine how experience shapes behavior, without proving that the entire model describes every action (O’Doherty, 2011; Purves et al., 2001).

A response learned in one situation can continue when the circumstances change. Avoidance that once reduced a real threat may later interrupt a conversation that could be manageable. The useful distinction is between what the response accomplished before and what its consequences are now.

This gives the broader model a way to examine why a response persists. Something can continue to feel necessary because it has repeatedly produced immediate relief, even when its later effects are costly. Asking about the learned expectation and the present consequence can reveal different parts of the pattern without reducing a person’s whole life to a single mechanism.

question: What did this response help you avoid or obtain before, and what does it do now?
